analysis.one_liner: Bans drugmakers from switching patients to a tweaked drug version to block cheap generics.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill on a bipartisan basis, but it never received a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name drug is about to lose its patent, some manufacturers 'product hop': they pull the old pill from the market or nudge doctors onto a slightly changed version, resetting the clock on their monopoly and delaying cheap generics. This bill would make that practice an unfair method of competition under the Federal Trade Commission Act, letting the FTC go after hard switches (withdrawing the old drug) and soft switches (unfairly steering patients to the new one). The committee approved it but the House never voted.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take brand-name drugs facing patent expiration. The bill would speed the arrival of cheaper generic and biosimilar versions by making it unlawful to yank the old drug or disadvantage it in favor of a reformulated follow-on, subject to safety and supply exceptions [S2][S3][S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients facing high brand-name drug prices

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits product hopping, presumed when a manufacturer removes a drug from the FDA's approved list, discontinues it, or markets a reformulation after being notified that a generic applicant has filed [S2][S3].

A 'hard switch' — getting FDA to withdraw the old drug, discontinuing it, or destroying inventory in a way that impedes generic competition — is treated as an unfair method of competition under the FTC Act [S4].

A 'soft switch' — other actions that unfairly disadvantage the old drug relative to a follow-on product while the manufacturer sells the follow-on — is also covered, so tactics short of outright withdrawal are caught too [S4].
The FTC enforces the ban, and the bill applies to conduct after enactment; it leaves existing antitrust laws intact so the change adds a tool rather than replacing old ones [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would lose the ability to extend monopoly pricing on a drug by swapping patients onto a reformulated version just before generics arrive. They would also face FTC enforcement and litigation risk, offset by exceptions for actions taken for patient-safety reasons or genuine supply disruptions [S4].

drawbacks.text: Reformulations are sometimes genuine improvements, so a broad presumption could deter legitimate changes to drugs. The bill tries to handle this by letting manufacturers justify their actions: hard switches are excused for patient-safety risks or supply disruptions outside the manufacturer's control, and soft switches for legitimate pro-competitive reasons; the FTC or a court can still reject a justification the conduct does not really need [S4].

Enforcement would require case-by-case fact findings by the FTC or courts about a manufacturer's intent and competitive effects, which means litigation costs and the possibility that some cases turn on contested evidence rather than a bright-line rule [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside — faster generic entry and lower prices on drugs where monopoly pricing would otherwise be extended — is large and falls on the public. The costs are mostly borne by brand-name manufacturers, and the bill's safety, supply, and pro-competitive-justification carve-outs address the main good-faith objection that not all reformulations are bad. On balance the design is targeted rather than sweeping; the main uncertainty is how FTC and courts apply the presumptions in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved it within days of introduction in 2019, but the report only came out on December 24, 2020, and the House never scheduled a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 18, 2019 by Rep. David Cicilline with original cosponsors including both Democratic and Republican leaders of the House Judiciary Committee [S1][S4].

The same day it was referred to the Judiciary Committee and its antitrust subcommittee, which was immediately discharged, and the committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported on November 21, 2019 [S6].
The committee report (H. Rept. 116-695) was not filed until December 24, 2020, when the bill was placed on the Union Calendar [S6].
The bill received no House floor vote and expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: with no law on the books, the ability to extend monopoly pricing by reformulating or withdrawing a drug ahead of generic competition stayed intact. Patients who would have paid the resulting higher prices are worse off.

sides.party_line_note: Support ran across the aisle: the original sponsors included the Judiciary chairman (Nadler) and its top Republicans (Collins and Sensenbrenner), and 3 of the 5 cosponsors were Republicans [S4][S5].

industries.note: Product hopping lets a maker keep monopoly prices on an old drug by shifting patients to a reformulated version right before generics arrive; the bill makes that an FTC-enforceable unfair practice [S2][S4]. Patients pay the difference for years when it succeeds.

The bill protects generic and biosimilar applicants from being locked out when a manufacturer withdraws or disadvantages the reference product after a generic application is filed, so cheaper copies reach patients sooner [S2][S4].
